title: Erdős Problem #1051: Irrationality of Reciprocal Product Series
description: If a₁ < a₂ < ⋯ are integers with lim inf aₙ^{1/2ⁿ} > 1, is Σ 1/(aₙ·aₙ₊₁) irrational? Known for rapid growth aₙ₊₁ ≥ C·aₙ². OPEN in general.

meta.author: Erdős
references: Erdős–Graham (1980), 'Old and New Problems and Results in Combinatorial Number Theory', p.64
Erdős (1988), 'On the irrationality of certain series: problems and results', pp.102–109
Sylvester (1880): the Sylvester sequence and Egyptian fraction expansions
Oppenheim (1953): irrationality of reciprocal sums of rapidly growing sequences

overview.historicalContext: Erdős and Ronald Graham posed this problem in their 1980 monograph 'Old and New Problems and Results in Combinatorial Number Theory' (p.64), asking about irrationality of series $\sum 1/(a_n a_{n+1})$ for rapidly growing integer sequences. The question connects to a classical theme in number theory: when does a convergent series of rationals sum to an irrational number? Alexander Oppenheim (1953) initiated the systematic study of such series, proving irrationality for specific growth rates. Erdős (1988) solved the case when $a_{n+1} \geq C \cdot a_n^2$ (quadratic recurrence), using the key observation that under such growth, the partial sums approximate the total sum so rapidly that no rational number can be close to all partial sums simultaneously. The general case—requiring only $\liminf a_n^{1/2^n} > 1$ (doubly exponential growth)—remains open. The gap between the quadratic recurrence and the general growth condition is substantial: sequences can grow doubly exponentially without satisfying $a_{n+1} \geq C a_n^2$ at every step. The Sylvester sequence $s_n$ (where $s_{n+1} = s_n^2 - s_n + 1$) provides a key example where both conditions hold and irrationality is verified via telescoping.
overview.problemStatement: If $a_1 < a_2 < \cdots$ is a strictly increasing sequence of integers with $\liminf_{n \to \infty} a_n^{1/2^n} > 1$, is $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{a_n \cdot a_{n+1}}$ irrational?
overview.proofStrategy: We formalize the growth condition using Mathlib's $\texttt{Filter.liminf}$, define the reciprocal product series via $\texttt{tsum}$, and state the conjecture as a universal irrationality claim. The solved rapid growth case ($a_{n+1} \geq C a_n^2$) is axiomatized along with convergence, positivity, the related simple reciprocal series conjecture, and the Sylvester–Fibonacci existence example.
keyInsights: **Doubly exponential growth**: The condition $\liminf a_n^{1/2^n} > 1$ means $a_n \geq \alpha^{2^n}$ eventually for some $\alpha > 1$—doubly exponential, but allowing irregular growth patterns

**Gap between known and conjectured**: Erdős (1988) proved irrationality for $a_{n+1} \geq C a_n^2$, which implies $a_n \geq C^{2^n-1} a_0^{2^n}$. The growth condition is strictly weaker, allowing $a_{n+1}$ to sometimes be much smaller than $a_n^2$
**Telescoping structure**: For Sylvester-type sequences, partial fractions give $1/(a_n a_{n+1}) = 1/(a_n - 1) - 1/(a_{n+1} - 1)$, making the sum telescoping—but general sequences lack this structure

**Irrationality via approximation speed**: The proof for rapid growth uses the fact that partial sums $S_N = \sum_{n=1}^{N} 1/(a_n a_{n+1})$ converge so fast to $S$ that no rational $p/q$ can satisfy $|S - p/q| < 1/q$ for all $q$
**Connection to Egyptian fractions**: The Sylvester sequence arises in greedy Egyptian fraction expansions of 1, connecting this problem to the representation theory of rationals

sections.title: Mathlib Imports
sections.summary: Imports integers, reals, the $\texttt{Irrational}$ predicate, $\texttt{Filter.liminf}$ for the growth condition, and $\texttt{tsum}$ for infinite series.

sections.title: Growth Condition
sections.summary: Defines $\texttt{GrowthCondition}(a)$: $\liminf_{n \to \infty} a_n^{1/2^n} > 1$, ensuring doubly exponential growth $a_n \geq \alpha^{2^n}$.

sections.title: The Reciprocal Product Series
sections.summary: Defines $S(a) = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} 1/(a_n \cdot a_{n+1})$ using Mathlib's $\texttt{tsum}$. The central quantity whose irrationality is in question.

sections.title: The Main Conjecture
sections.summary: States $\texttt{ErdosProblem1051}$: for all strictly monotone integer sequences with the growth condition, $S(a)$ is irrational.

sections.title: Rapid Growth Case (Solved)
sections.summary: Erdős (1988): irrationality holds when $a_{n+1} \geq C \cdot a_n^2$. The strongest known result toward the full conjecture.

sections.title: Convergence and Positivity
sections.summary: Under the growth condition, $S(a)$ converges absolutely (terms decay as $\alpha^{-3 \cdot 2^n}$). Positive when all $a_n > 0$.

sections.title: Related Series Questions
sections.summary: The companion series $T(a) = \sum 1/a_n$ is also conjectured irrational under the same growth condition. A distinct but related open problem.

sections.title: Sylvester–Fibonacci Example
sections.summary: Existence example: the Sylvester sequence $s_{n+1} = s_n^2 - s_n + 1$ satisfies both conditions, with $S(s)$ provably irrational via telescoping.

conclusion.summary: This formalization captures Erdős Problem #1051 on the irrationality of $\sum 1/(a_n a_{n+1})$ for doubly-exponentially growing integer sequences. The Lean file encodes the growth condition via $\texttt{Filter.liminf}$, the series definition, the main conjecture, the solved rapid growth case (Erdős 1988), convergence and positivity properties, the companion simple series question, and a Sylvester–Fibonacci existence example.
conclusion.implications: A resolution would advance the theory of irrationality of series with integer terms, establishing a precise boundary between growth conditions that force irrationality and those that permit rational sums. It connects to deeper questions about Diophantine approximation speed and lacunary series.
openQuestions: Is $\sum 1/(a_n a_{n+1})$ irrational for all strictly increasing integer sequences with $\liminf a_n^{1/2^n} > 1$? (The main conjecture)
Is $\sum 1/a_n$ also irrational under the same growth condition? (The companion problem)
What is the weakest growth condition on $(a_n)$ that ensures irrationality of $\sum 1/(a_n a_{n+1})$?
Can the gap between the general growth condition and the quadratic recurrence $a_{n+1} \geq C a_n^2$ be narrowed by proving irrationality for intermediate growth rates?
